title: Why does oxygen have the wrong name? | ELEMENTS

entries.note: Means water-forming, correctly named because it forms water with oxygen; its ending is [[from:-gen]].
Ending meaning forming or generating, found in many element names; related to [[same-root:generation]] and [[same-root:generator]], and more loosely to [[same-root:gender]].
Related to the [[same-root:-gen]] ending, so hydrogen is a kind of water generator.
Related to [[same-root:-gen]]; the hosts gloss hydrogen as water generator.
More indirectly linked to the [[same-root:-gen]] ending.
More indirectly linked to the [[same-root:-gen]] ending.
More indirectly linked to the [[same-root:-gen]] ending.
The German word for [[equivalent:hydrogen]]; here [[see:stuff]] means material.
German Stoff means material; English stuff once meant the essence or material of something, as in [[see:the stuff of legend]], before becoming casual.
Example of [[see:stuff]] in its older sense of essential material.
The German word for [[equivalent:oxygen]], echoing the Greek idea of something sour or acid.
From Greek [[from:oxys]], sour or acid, meaning acid generator, from the mistaken belief it was needed to form acids; formerly called [[see:dephlogisticated air]].
Related to [[same-root:oxygen]] through the idea of sourness.
Related to [[same-root:oxygen]] and [[same-root:acid]].
Related to [[same-root:oxygen]] and [[same-root:acid]].
French word for sour, related to [[same-root:oxygen]] and found in [[gave:vinegar]].
Means sour wine, so it is related to [[same-root:oxygen]] via French [[from:aigre]].
Former name for [[see:oxygen]] given by [[see:Joseph Priestley]], meaning air lacking [[from:phlogiston]]; the hosts debate its pronunciation.
Mysterious substance of 1700s theory, thought abundant in combustible things and released into the air when they burned, leaving ash as their true form.
Jess's surname, which sounds like Latin for iron and Arabic for knight, but really comes from a Scottish name meaning strong or loyal man.
Generator of niter, from Greek [[from:nitron]], sodium carbonate, because the gas was identified in nitric acid and potassium nitrate.
Name for several alkaline substances, such as baking soda (sodium bicarbonate, an antacid) and soda ash (sodium carbonate, a water softener).
From [[from:potash]]; its symbol K comes from Latin [[from:kalium]].
Wood or plant ash soaked in a pot, long used for soap-making; gave us [[gave:potassium]].
Latin name behind potassium's symbol K, from a word for potash ultimately from Arabic [[from:al-qali]], which also gave [[same-root:alkali]].
From Arabic [[from:al-qali]], like [[same-root:kalium]].
A Germanic element name; its symbol Fe comes from Latin [[from:ferrum]].
Describes something made of iron, from Latin [[from:ferrum]]; punned on Jess's surname [[see:Ferris]].
Rob's surname, etymologically the same as [[same-root:Watson]], meaning son of Wat; Rob calls it a peasanty name.
Like [[same-root:Watts]], means son of Wat.
Symbol Au from Latin [[from:aurum]]; the word gold shares an origin with [[same-root:yellow]], words for bright, as discussed in their colour episode.
Comes from the same place as [[same-root:gold]], both tracing back to an h sound.
Its symbol Ag comes from Latin [[from:argentum]].
Named by Spanish colonists who found silver there, after Latin [[from:argentum]] rather than Spanish [[see:plata]].
Spanish for silver, not used for [[see:Argentina]] but the source of [[gave:platinum]].
From Spanish [[from:platina]], little silver, a diminutive of [[from:plata]].
Named after the Roman god [[from:Mercury]], linked to swift [[see:Hermes]]; also called [[see:quicksilver]], with symbol Hg from [[from:hydrargyrum]].
Another name for [[see:mercury]]; here [[see:quick]] means liquid or alive rather than speedy.
Can mean moving fast or alive, as in [[see:the quick and the dead]].
Phrase showing [[see:quick]] meaning alive; the hosts think they discussed it before.
Greek god associated with the Roman Mercury, a very fast traveller, explaining [[see:mercury]]'s name.
Modern Latin hybrid of Greek hydr- and Latin [[from:argentum]], source of mercury's symbol Hg.
Ending usually used to coin metal names, though non-metal [[see:helium]] has it too.
Named after sun god [[from:Helios]] because it was identified in the sun's corona before being obtained; assumed to be a metal, hence [[see:-ium]].
Symbol Pb from Latin [[from:plumbum]], which also gave [[same-root:plumber]] and [[same-root:plumb line]].
Plumbers originally worked with lead, from [[from:plumbum]] via French [[from:plombier]]; Renaissance scholars reinserted the silent B to show off the Latin.
Related to [[same-root:plumbum]], since pipes were made of lead.
A dangled piece of lead used to check something is straight, from [[from:plumbum]].
Latin for someone who smelted or worked with lead, the background to [[gave:plumber]].
Jess suggests it explains [[see:plumber]]'s silent B; Rob says it's Renaissance respelling, though it may explain [[see:dumb]].
French form that came into English without a B, giving [[gave:plumber]]; French also later reinserted the B.
Another word with a silent final MB, compared with [[see:plumber]].
Another word with a silent final MB, compared with [[see:plumber]].
Another word with a silent final MB, compared with [[see:plumber]].
Swedish for perhaps hard stone, though Swedish calls the element wolfram; its symbol W comes from [[see:Wolfram]].
Former English name for [[see:tungsten]].
German name for tungsten, behind the symbol W; perhaps an old mining nickname meaning wolf's cream, or more plausibly wolf's soot or dirt.
From German [[from:Kobold]], goblin, because arsenic-laced cobalt ore made miners ill; also discussed in their colour episode.
A small, mischievous goblin; miners believed kobolds treated well would knock to warn of mine collapses, probably really creaking rock. Gave [[gave:cobalt]].
Shortened from [[from:Kupfernickel]], false copper or copper goblin, because the ore was mistaken for copper; contains the demon [[see:Nick]].
Swedish or German name meaning false copper or copper imp, source of [[gave:nickel]]; not to be confused with [[see:copernicium]].
A demon or goblin, regularly a nickname for the devil, discussed in an earlier episode; found in [[gave:nickel]] and [[gave:pumpernickel]].
Means devil's fart or fart goblin, containing the same [[see:Nick]] as [[see:nickel]].
Means hidden; one of several elements named in 1898 to allude to their having gone undiscovered.
Means new; discovered by [[see:William Ramsay]] and [[see:Morris Travers]], who also found it glows in glass tubes, soon used for neon signs.
The stranger gas, related to [[same-root:xenophobia]]; strange because it is unusually reactive for one of the [[see:noble gases]] and was discovered late.
Fear of the strange or foreign, related to [[same-root:xenon]].
So called because they are unreactive and stable, well behaved like nobility, or too good to hang out with other elements.
The only element named after a living person, Russian chemist [[from:Yuri Oganessian]], aged 91.
Named after [[from:Tennessee]], Jess's home state; also found by [[see:Yuri Oganessian]].
So named because it is a decay product of [[from:radium]].
Named by [[see:Marie Curie]] and her husband; related to [[same-root:radioactive]], [[same-root:ray]] and [[same-root:radius]].
Related to [[same-root:radium]].
Related to [[same-root:radium]].
Related to [[same-root:radium]].
Named after [[from:Marie Curie]] and [[from:Pierre Curie]].
Named after Poland, the home country of [[see:Marie Curie]].
Polish patriot often assumed French, which may have irritated her; her real name was Maria Skłodowska-Curie, and [[gave:curium]] and [[gave:polonium]] honour her.
Named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm; also discovered in [[see:Ytterby]].
Small village on Sweden's Baltic coast with the most elements named after it; a Stockholm barista taught Rob its Germanic Y pronunciation.
One of four elements named directly after [[from:Ytterby]].
One of four elements named directly after [[from:Ytterby]].
One of four elements named directly after [[from:Ytterby]].
One of four elements named directly after [[from:Ytterby]].
Discovered in [[see:Ytterby]] and given a geographical Scandinavian name, prompting [[see:thulium]] for a later find.
Found in [[see:Ytterby]] and named after [[from:Thule]] since scandium was already taken.
Greek and Latin word for the northernmost reaches of civilisation, a byword for Scandinavia; gave [[gave:thulium]].
Group including the [[see:Ytterby]] elements; found together and fairly common, but rarely concentrated enough to extract easily.
From Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, whose name contains a word meaning harbour.
Named after [[from:Lutetia]], the Gallo-Roman town that preceded Paris.
Listed among elements named after places.
Listed among elements named after places.
Presumably named after [[from:Berkeley]].
Named after [[from:Darmstadt]] in Germany.
Named after [[from:Strontian]] in Scotland.
Possibly named after [[from?:Cyprus]] via Roman [[from?:aes cyprium]], but it's unclear whether the island or the metal came first.
Major Roman copper source; from Greek Kypros, possibly land of [[from?:cypress]] trees, or else the tree is named after the island.
Roman name for the metal, suggesting [[gave?:copper]] is named after [[from:Cyprus]].
Tree from Greek kyparissos, related to [[same-root?:Cyprus]], though it's unclear which named which; the spelling difference goes unexplained.
Named after a word meaning shy, because it was hard to find.
Named after a word meaning shy, because it was hard to find.
The lazy element, meaning not working; related to [[same-root:synergy]], [[same-root:ergonomic]] and [[same-root:organize]], but unrelated to [[unrelated:Argo]].
The ship, whose name means quick, unrelated to [[unrelated:argon]].
Means working together, related to [[same-root:argon]]; not corporate jargon but an old biblical Greek term, like [[equivalent:collaboration]].
Related to [[same-root:argon]] through the idea of work.
Related to [[same-root:argon]] through the idea of work.
Also literally means working together, like [[see:synergy]].
Means the stinky one, perhaps unfairly, since the compound being worked on may have stunk rather than osmium itself.
Another smelly element, from Greek [[from:bromos]], stench.
Commenters argue over pronouncing it zoo-ology or zo-ology; Jess switches between them, and Rob sticks with zo-ology.
Berlin's western station, Bahnhof Zoo, is named for the zoo; in German, Zoo is pronounced with a ts sound.
Probably from a root meaning to burn; associated with hell and also called [[see:brimstone]].
Other name for [[see:sulfur]], meaning stone that burns.
Named after [[from:Tantalus]] because it resists absorption in acid, as Tantalus is denied water; found in Ytterby.
Greek figure condemned to stand chin-deep in water he can't drink, beneath fruit he can't reach; gave [[gave:tantalum]], and his daughter inspired [[see:niobium]].
Named after [[from:Niobe]], daughter of [[see:Tantalus]], by [[see:Heinrich Rose]], who found it in [[see:tantalite]], so it's like tantalum's offspring.
Mineral that is the source of both [[see:tantalum]] and [[see:niobium]].
Named after the [[from:Titans]], perhaps for its strength or because they were sons of the earth.
Named after [[from:Prometheus]], found during the Manhattan Project; perhaps warning of punishment by nuclear war, or because it was punishingly hard to synthesise.
Named after [[from:Cadmus]], via Cadmea, the Theban citadel where he supposedly ruled.
Legendary founder of Thebes, supposedly responsible for bringing the Phoenician alphabet to the Greeks; gave [[gave:cadmium]].
Element named after [[from:Pallas Athena]]; also a word for a safeguard, from an image of Athena protecting Troy, and a common venue name.
Named after the Norse god [[from:Thor]].
Named after one of the many names for [[from:Freyja]].
Means light-bearer because it glows; Phosphoros was also a Greek god linked to Venus, and the name later became associated with [[see:Lucifer]].
Associated with Phosphoros through the Greek Bible, part of [[see:phosphorus]]'s connections.
Named after the planet Pluto, so only mythology-adjacent.
Named after the planet Neptune.
Named after the planet Uranus.
Named after the moon, [[from:Selene]] also being a moon goddess.
Ancient concept of a thing granting eternal life and turning lead into gold; [[see:elixir]] named the same idea.

entries.term: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
entries.note: Retitled the Sorcerer's Stone in America, apparently because publishers doubted children knew what a [[see:philosopher's stone]] was.
Was also a word for the same concept as the [[see:philosopher's stone]].
Linked to [[from:Magnesia]]; its coiner tried to avoid the confusion with [[see:magnium]], but magnesium stuck anyway.
Also named after [[from:Magnesia]] and oddly corrupted; used to remove colour in glassmaking and weakly paramagnetic.
Named after [[from:Magnesia]], where a magnetic mineral was supposedly first found.
Named after [[from:Magnesia]], like [[same-root:magnet]].
District of Thessaly, Greece, where a magnetic mineral was supposedly first found; source of [[gave:magnet]], [[gave:manganese]] and [[gave:magnesium]].
Name the coiner of [[see:magnesium]] preferred, to avoid confusion with [[see:Magnesia]]; it didn't catch on.
Named after sky blue, one of several elements named after colours.
Garbled in the captions; apparently named after a greenish-yellow colour.
From the Greek for violet.
Named after [[from:indigo]] rather than directly after India.
Named after India; gave [[gave:indium]].
Ultimately from a Persian word for gold-coloured; an arsenic sulfide mineral has a distinctive golden colour.
From a Greek word meaning rose-coloured.
Means deep red, from the red lines in its spectrum, like [[same-root:ruby]].
Compared with [[see:rubidium]], deep red.
Symbol Sn comes from Latin [[from:stannum]], simply the word for tin.
One of a collection of elements named after scientists.
Named after [[from:Copernicus]]; not to be confused with [[see:Kupfernickel]].
Named after Dane [[from:Niels Bohr]], who mapped atomic structure and was a big name in quantum theory.
Means uncut or indivisible, so related to [[same-root:anatomy]].
Literally a cutting up or dissection, related to [[same-root:atom]].
Named after Russian scientist [[from:Dmitri Mendeleev]].
Named after Moscow; one of the elements linked to Russia.
From Ruthenia, the Latin name for Russia.
Means not alone because it's found in many compounds, the pro-social element; symbol Sb from Latin [[from:stibium]].
Named because it flows; it was used as a [[see:flux]] in smelting to remove impurities and make metals more fluid.
Also meaning flow, a smelting substance; explains [[see:fluorine]].
From the Latin for coal or charcoal; many European words for coal resemble it.
Jess's favourite: named after [[from:beryl]], the gemstone group it was extracted from; Rob had assumed it was named after a woman called Beryl.
Gemstone category including emerald, aquamarine, goshenite, morganite and [[see:red beryl]]; related to [[same-root:brilliant]] and German [[same-root:Brille]].
Literally means shining like [[from:beryl]].
German word for glasses, related to [[same-root:beryl]].
An example of a [[see:beryl]].
An example of a [[see:beryl]].
An example of a [[see:beryl]].
An example of a [[see:beryl]].
A [[see:beryl]] formerly called bixbite, after [[from:Maynard Bixby]].
Arranged in [[from:period]]s because element properties recur at intervals down the rows.
From Greek periodos, circuit or cycle; it can mean a span, and in the full-stop sense a complete cycle of speech or writing.
